chunks: "Ambient light affects a camera in three ways: how much, what color, and how steady. How much is the big one.
A scene in full sun is around 100,000 lux, an office is about 500, a dim living room is 50 and a street at night is a few lux.
The signal the sensor collects scales with that, and photon shot noise means SNR goes as the square root of the signal.
So in the dark, the image gets noisy, the camera has to use long exposures that blur, and it cranks gain.
Autofocus also gets slower or fails because contrast and phase signals drop.
What color matters because different lights have different spectra: daylight is around 6500 K, incandescent is 2700 K, and some LEDs have spiky spectra.
The sensor just sees raw red, green and blue, so the ISP has to estimate the illuminant and apply white balance, and under bad spectra the colors come out wrong or the blue channel is noisy.
How steady matters because mains lights flicker at 100 or 120 hertz, and PWM-dimmed LEDs even faster.
If the exposure isn't a multiple of the flicker period, or with a rolling shutter, you get brightness banding across the frame.
On top of that, scenes with strong contrast, like a backlit person, exceed the sensor's dynamic range, so you need HDR, and bright sources cause glare and lens flare."
